arguments.heading: Argument analysis: March 24, 2026 session
paragraphs: This was the only argument session, held March 24, 2026. Vivek Suri argued for the government. Kelsi B. Corkran argued for Al Otro Lado. No reargument occurred, so nothing changed on a second round.

The government asked the Court to reverse the Ninth Circuit and uphold metering, and to lift the class-wide declaration and individual injunction. Its reasoning: the statute requires presence on U.S. soil; one law covers refugees outside the country; Sale supports extraterritorial limits; duties are shared internationally. The justices tested assumptions about whether the government's reading makes words redundant, why Congress would favor unlawful entrants, and whether metering is lawful without capacity limits.

Al Otro Lado asked the Court to read the statute to require processing for people who arrive, including those at the border. Its reasoning: turn-backs began around 2016 to avoid processing duties; arrival happens at the threshold; regulations and Thuraissigiam support this. The justices tested assumptions about where arrival begins, whether treaty duties are implicated, and whether the reading rewards unlawful entry.

On mootness, the government said the class-wide declaration keeps the case live and lifting it gives real relief, and that recurrence is reasonably expected. It said it wants the ability to reinstate metering if justified. Justice Barrett asked whether the agency plans to reinstate metering. Justice Jackson raised the advisory opinion concern. Al Otro Lado did not object to Munsingwear vacatur.
The approved record does not support additional arguments, facts, or responses beyond those listed here.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case involves a border policy called metering. Metering means officers only let a limited number of people approach the border to ask for protection. The government says it can do this. A group called Al Otro Lado says the policy breaks federal law. The fight is over what the word arrives means in the immigration statute.
The lawyers were Vivek Suri for the government and Kelsi B. Corkran for Al Otro Lado.

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 1, lines 1-9

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: A lower court ruled against the government. The government brought the case to the Supreme Court. The case includes a class-wide declaration covering many people, plus an individual order for one person called Beatrice Doe. The government says the class-wide order is still active. The Court heard oral argument on March 24, 2026.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: The government asks the Court to reverse the Ninth Circuit and uphold the metering policy. It also asks the Court to lift the class-wide declaration and the individual injunction. Al Otro Lado's side did not object to a certain type of vacatur called Munsingwear vacatur, which would set the ruling aside while the case stays pending.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: The government argues the law's phrase arrives in the United States requires a person to be on American soil. It says one part of the law covers refugees outside the country, and another covers people already inside. It leans on an earlier case called Sale for limits that reach beyond U.S. borders. It also says the government can share international duties with Mexico, with bigger duties once someone is inside.

Al Otro Lado argues the law requires processing for people who arrive, and that turning people back counts as harmful refoulement. It says turn-backs began around 2016 to dodge processing duties. It leans on regulations and an earlier case called Thuraissigiam. It says arrival happens at the threshold, even before someone steps over the line.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Sotomayor asked about the scope of the Sale case and whether treaty duties conflict with metering. She also noted a government watchdog report suggesting metering may have been used as cover. Justice Thomas asked how this case differs from Sale and whether treaty obligations are involved.

Justice Kagan asked whether the government's reading makes part of the law redundant, and whether the right at the border means applying for protection or actually crossing. Justice Alito asked how to handle over-capacity when metering stops, and explored door and threshold analogies for the word arrives.

Justice Kavanaugh asked why Congress would give unlawful entrants an advantage over people who follow the rules, and whether metering is lawful when there is no capacity problem. Justice Barrett asked where arrives begins, using proximity and queue examples, and whether the agency plans to reinstate metering.
Justice Jackson raised concerns about mootness and about rewarding people who enter unlawfully to seek asylum.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: The case decides whether the government can keep people away from the border before they reach it. If the law covers people at the threshold, metering may be unlawful. If it covers only people on U.S. soil, metering may stand. The answer shapes how thousands of people can seek protection.

The government also disputes the factual premise behind the lower court's ruling, saying the case is not a simple summary-judgment situation. It says the facial challenge to metering is before the Court, but a separate claim about arbitrary policy is not.

sections.heading: What happens next
paragraphs: The Court heard argument and will decide the case later. A question from a justice is not a ruling or a vote. The government asks for reversal and lifting of the orders. Al Otro Lado asks for the law to be read to require processing at the border. The approved record does not support any prediction about the result.
